questions.q: Which task is the best use case for the Researcher agent?
options: Calculating the sum of a column in a spreadsheet
Assigning Microsoft 365 licences to a group
Resetting a user's password
Producing a multi-step research report on a market opportunity, combining internal work data with web sources
questions.explain: Researcher is a reasoning agent built for deep, multi-step research. It plans, searches across your work data and the web (including connected third-party sources), and produces a structured, cited report rather than a quick answer.

wrong.0: That is a simple calculation - Analyst or a formula would be overkill or better suited.
wrong.1: Licensing is done in the Microsoft 365 admin center.
wrong.2: Password resets are an admin task in Entra ID.

questions.q: Which task is the best use case for the Analyst agent?
options: Turning several raw spreadsheets into a demand forecast with visualisations, showing its reasoning
Applying a sensitivity label to a document
Scheduling a recurring meeting
Drafting a company newsletter
questions.explain: Analyst is the data-focused reasoning agent. It works through raw data step by step, can run Python to do the analysis, and returns insights, forecasts and visualisations along with the work it did to get there.

wrong.1: Labelling is a Purview Information Protection action.
wrong.2: Scheduling is a calendar task.
wrong.3: Newsletter drafting is standard Copilot writing help.

questions.q: A finance team needs revenue projections built from four internal spreadsheets. Which should they use?
options: Analyst, because the work is quantitative analysis of raw data
Communication Compliance, because finance data is sensitive
Copilot Studio, because a custom agent is always required
Researcher, because it can browse the web
questions.explain: Analyst specialises in quantitative work on raw data - exactly what building projections from spreadsheets is. Researcher is the right choice when the task is synthesising information from many sources including the web.

wrong.1: Communication Compliance reviews messages for policy violations.
wrong.2: Built-in agents cover this without any custom build.
wrong.3: Web browsing is not what this task needs.

cues: revenue projections built from four internal spreadsheets

questions.q: Which scenario best justifies building a custom agent rather than using Copilot directly?
options: A manager wants to rewrite a paragraph in a Word document
HR wants a consistent assistant that answers only from approved policy documents and follows a fixed tone
A user wants to summarise the email they are reading
An analyst wants to build a chart from a table in Excel
questions.explain: Custom agents earn their keep when you need repeatable, scoped behaviour: a defined knowledge boundary, specific instructions, and the same answer style every time for many users.

wrong.0: That is everyday Copilot in Word.
wrong.2: That is everyday Copilot in Outlook.
wrong.3: That is Copilot in Excel or the Analyst agent.

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes the two main commercial models for Copilot capabilities?
options: A fixed monthly per-user licence for Microsoft 365 Copilot, and pay-as-you-go consumption billing for experiences such as SharePoint agents and Copilot Chat agents
A one-off perpetual licence and an annual maintenance fee
Per-device licensing and per-server licensing
A free tier only, with no paid options
questions.explain: Microsoft 365 Copilot is a per-user subscription with predictable monthly cost. Alongside it, pay-as-you-go lets people use certain agent experiences without a full licence, billed by consumption through an Azure subscription.

wrong.1: Microsoft 365 is subscription-based, not perpetual.
wrong.2: Copilot is licensed per user, not per device or server.
wrong.3: There are clearly paid options.

questions.q: Which experiences can be billed on a pay-as-you-go basis?
options: Microsoft Entra ID P1 licences
Windows 11 upgrades
Microsoft Copilot Chat agents, SharePoint agents and the Copilot Retrieval API
Exchange Online mailboxes
questions.explain: Pay-as-you-go covers Copilot Chat, SharePoint agents and the Retrieval API, letting users who do not have a full Copilot licence use those agent experiences with usage billed to an Azure subscription.

wrong.0: Entra licences are per-user subscriptions.
wrong.1: Operating system licensing is unrelated.
wrong.3: Mailboxes come with Microsoft 365 subscriptions.

questions.q: What does a billing policy do in the Microsoft 365 admin center?
options: Controls which sensitivity labels are available
Sets the retention period for Copilot prompts
Links a group of users to an Azure subscription so their pay-as-you-go Copilot usage is billed to the right cost centre, and grants those users access to the service
Assigns Microsoft 365 Copilot licences automatically
questions.explain: A billing policy is the connection between people and money: it names the Azure subscription that pays, scopes which users or groups it covers, and controls their access to the pay-as-you-go service. Disconnect the policy and those users lose access.

wrong.0: Labels are configured in Purview.
wrong.1: Retention is a Purview setting.
wrong.3: Subscription licences are assigned separately under Users or Billing.

questions.q: Which admin roles can create and manage pay-as-you-go billing policies for Copilot?
options: Any licensed Copilot user
Global Administrator, Billing Administrator or AI Administrator (Global Reader can view)
Teams channel moderators
SharePoint site owners
questions.explain: Billing policies affect spend, so they are restricted to Global Administrator, Billing Administrator and AI Administrator. Global Reader can see them but cannot change them.

wrong.0: Ordinary users cannot commit the organisation to spend.
wrong.2: Channel moderation is a Teams content role.
wrong.3: Site ownership grants no tenant billing rights.

questions.q: An organisation wants to prevent unexpected pay-as-you-go Copilot spend. Which controls are available?
options: Reducing every user's mailbox quota
Deleting the Azure subscription each month
Budgets with email alerts at spending thresholds, and hard caps that stop consumption
Disabling multifactor authentication for billing admins
questions.explain: The cost management experience in the Microsoft 365 admin center lets you track consumption, set budgets that alert at percentage milestones, and apply hard caps so usage stops rather than running over budget.

wrong.0: Mailbox size has nothing to do with AI consumption.
wrong.1: Deleting the subscription would break the service entirely.
wrong.3: Weakening authentication is a security risk, not a cost control.

questions.q: What is the correct way to give 50 users Microsoft 365 Copilot?
options: Install a Copilot add-in on each user's device
Add the users to the Global Administrator role
Assign the Copilot licence to the users directly or to a group they belong to in the Microsoft 365 admin center
Create a conditional access policy that includes those users
questions.explain: Copilot is switched on for a person by assigning the licence, either one by one under Active users or, more efficiently, through group-based licensing.

wrong.0: There is nothing to install - Copilot is part of the service.
wrong.1: Admin roles grant management rights, not product features, and this would be a serious over-permission.
wrong.3: Conditional access controls how users sign in, not what they are licensed for.

questions.q: Which of these Copilot behaviours can an administrator turn on or off for the organisation?
options: Whether Copilot honours SharePoint permissions
Whether prompts are used to train the foundation models
Whether Copilot can use web content to ground its responses
Whether Microsoft Graph exists in the tenant
questions.explain: Web grounding is an admin-controlled setting - some organisations require answers to come only from internal data. Admins can also control agent access, plugins and connectors, and which apps show Copilot features.

wrong.0: Permission enforcement is fundamental and cannot be disabled.
wrong.1: Prompts are never used for foundation model training, so there is no switch.
wrong.3: Graph is core platform infrastructure, not an optional feature.

cues: turn on or off for the organisation

questions.q: What is the Copilot Control System?
options: A separate licence purchased per agent
A hardware appliance installed in the datacentre
A replacement for Microsoft Purview
Microsoft's governance framework for securing, managing and measuring Copilot and agents, spanning the Microsoft 365 admin center, Power Platform admin center and Copilot Studio
questions.explain: The Copilot Control System groups the admin capabilities into three pillars: security and governance, management controls (licensing and metering, agent lifecycle, customisation), and measurement and reporting.

wrong.0: It is not a separately purchased product.
wrong.1: It is entirely a cloud management capability.
wrong.2: It works alongside Purview rather than replacing it.

questions.q: An administrator wants only the Finance department to be able to use agents. Where is this configured?
options: In SharePoint site permissions
In the Exchange admin center mail flow rules
In the Microsoft 365 admin center Copilot settings, under data access for agents, scoping access to specific users or groups
In the Teams meeting policy
questions.explain: Agent access is set in Copilot settings, where you choose whether all users, no users, or only specific users and groups can use agents. You can also restrict which publishers of agents are allowed.

wrong.0: Site permissions control content access, not agent availability.
wrong.1: Mail flow rules control email routing.
wrong.3: Meeting policies control meeting features.

questions.q: What is the difference between making an agent 'available to' users and 'deploying' it to them?
options: There is no difference
Available applies to Teams; deployed applies to Outlook
Available means free; deployed means paid
Available means users can find and install it themselves; deployed means the admin installs it on their behalf
questions.explain: Availability is discovery - the agent shows up in the store for those users if they want it. Deployment is a push: the admin installs it for the users or groups, accepting the required permissions on their behalf, so it is simply there.

wrong.0: The distinction matters for rollout planning.
wrong.1: Both settings work across the supported apps.
wrong.2: Neither term relates to price.

questions.q: A maker publishes an agent from Copilot Studio to the organisation. What happens next?
options: It is deleted unless the maker has a Copilot licence
It becomes instantly available to every user in the tenant
Microsoft reviews and approves it on the organisation's behalf
The agent appears as a request in the Microsoft 365 admin center, where an admin reviews it and publishes or rejects it
questions.explain: Publishing to the organisation creates a request, not a live agent. An admin reviews its metadata, its knowledge and actions, and its security and compliance details, then publishes it to the catalogue or rejects it.

wrong.0: Licensing does not delete submitted agents.
wrong.1: Automatic tenant-wide availability would defeat the purpose of governance.
wrong.2: The approval decision belongs to the customer's admins.

questions.q: When reviewing a requested agent, which details should an administrator examine before approving it?
options: Only the agent's icon and name
How many Teams channels the maker belongs to
The maker's mailbox size
Its knowledge sources, capabilities and actions, plus its security and compliance information and whether it has an owner
questions.explain: Approval is a risk decision. The data and tools view shows what the agent can reach and do, the security and compliance view shows certification and data handling, and an agent without an owner is a maintenance risk later.

wrong.0: Cosmetic details tell you nothing about risk.
wrong.1: Channel membership is irrelevant.
wrong.2: Mailbox size is irrelevant.

questions.q: Which Microsoft 365 admin center view shows every agent in the tenant, who it is available to, and which agents have no owner?
options: The SharePoint data access governance report
The Entra sign-in logs
The agent inventory under Agents > All agents
Compliance Manager
questions.explain: The agent inventory is the single list of agents: name, publisher, availability, which products support it, and filters such as 'missing an owner' so you can find abandoned agents to clean up.

wrong.0: DAG reports cover SharePoint sharing exposure.
wrong.1: Sign-in logs cover authentication.
wrong.3: Compliance Manager scores regulatory readiness.

questions.q: An agent from an external publisher is judged unacceptable and must never be usable in the tenant. What should the admin do?
options: Block the agent so no one in the organisation can access it
Delete the SharePoint site the agent references
Remove the maker's Copilot licence
Add the agent to the pinned agents list
questions.explain: Blocking prevents any access to that agent tenant-wide. Removing an agent simply takes it out of the inventory and it could be added again from the store, so blocking is the right action for something you want kept out.

wrong.1: Deleting content is destructive and does not block the agent.
wrong.2: Licence removal affects a person, not the agent.
wrong.3: Pinning promotes an agent - the exact opposite.

cues: judged unacceptable and must never be usable in the tenant

questions.q: Which admin roles can manage agents in the Microsoft 365 admin center?
options: Any user with a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence
AI Administrator and Global Administrator, with Global Reader able to view
Teams meeting organisers
SharePoint site members
questions.explain: Agent management is a privileged task. The AI Administrator role exists specifically for Copilot and agent administration, Global Administrator has it inherently, and Global Reader gets read-only visibility.

wrong.0: A licence grants use, not administration.
wrong.2: Meeting roles are unrelated.
wrong.3: Site membership is a content permission.

questions.q: Where does an administrator manage governance settings and environments for agents built in Copilot Studio?
options: The Power Platform admin center
The SharePoint admin center
The Exchange admin center
The Microsoft Purview portal
questions.explain: Copilot Studio agents live in Power Platform environments, so the Power Platform admin center is where environments, data loss prevention policies for connectors, capacity and Copilot Studio governance settings are managed.

wrong.1: SharePoint manages sites and content.
wrong.2: Exchange manages mail.
wrong.3: Purview handles compliance across data, not Power Platform environments.

questions.q: Which reporting capability gives leadership a view of Copilot adoption, usage trends and productivity impact?
options: The unified audit log
Identity Secure Score
Copilot Analytics, including the Copilot Dashboard in Viva Insights and usage reports in the Microsoft 365 admin center
The message center
questions.explain: Copilot Analytics is the reporting layer: the admin center shows licences, activation and usage by app, while the Copilot Dashboard in Viva Insights adds adoption and impact insights, and Viva Insights advanced reports cover business value.

wrong.0: The audit log records individual actions for investigations.
wrong.1: Secure Score rates identity configuration.
wrong.3: The message center announces service changes.

cues: adoption, usage trends and productivity impact

questions.q: An admin needs to know how many assigned Copilot licences are actually being used each month, broken down by app. Where should they look?
options: The Microsoft 365 Copilot usage report in the Microsoft 365 admin center
The SharePoint recycle bin
Entra sign-in logs
Content explorer in Purview
questions.explain: The Copilot usage report in the admin center shows enabled users, active users and activity per app (Teams, Word, Outlook, Excel, PowerPoint), which is how you spot unused licences worth reassigning.

wrong.1: The recycle bin holds deleted items.
wrong.2: Sign-in logs show authentication events, not feature usage.
wrong.3: Content explorer inventories sensitive data.

questions.q: Which information does agent monitoring in the admin center provide?
options: Usage and operational insights per agent, plus lifecycle status such as availability, ownership and consumption
The credit card details of the maker
The contents of every conversation with the agent, shown to all admins by default
The source code of every agent
questions.explain: Agent reporting covers who is using which agents, how much they are consuming, and their lifecycle state. Conversation content is governed through Purview for compliance purposes, not exposed casually in usage dashboards.

wrong.1: Payment details are never exposed in agent reporting.
wrong.2: Conversation content is compliance-controlled, not a default admin dashboard.
wrong.3: Source code is not surfaced this way.

questions.q: What are organisational prompts in Microsoft Copilot?
options: Prompts that an administrator creates and publishes so they are suggested to users in Copilot Chat, Teams and Edge
Prompts stored only on a user's local device
Prompts automatically generated by Microsoft for all tenants
Prompts that agents send to administrators for approval
questions.explain: Organisational prompts are curated by admins in the Microsoft 365 admin center under Copilot > Prompts. They appear as suggested prompts, in the prompt lab, and as typeahead suggestions, which is a simple way to spread good practice.

wrong.1: They are published centrally to users, not stored locally.
wrong.2: Microsoft provides samples, but organisational prompts are created by your own admins.
wrong.3: Prompts are not an approval mechanism.

questions.q: Which roles can create and manage organisational prompts in the Microsoft 365 admin center?
options: AI Administrator or Search Editor
Exchange recipient administrator
Any licensed user
Teams device administrator
questions.explain: Publishing prompts to everyone is an administrative act, so it is limited to the AI Administrator and Search Editor roles working in the admin center under Copilot > Prompts.

wrong.1: That role manages mail recipients.
wrong.2: Users can save their own prompts, but not publish organisation-wide ones.
wrong.3: That role manages Teams hardware.

questions.q: What do scheduled prompts allow a user to do?
options: Reserve Copilot capacity for a future date
Run a chosen prompt automatically at a set time or frequency, with the results delivered in Copilot experiences such as Teams and Outlook
Send a prompt to an administrator for approval
Schedule a Teams meeting from a prompt
questions.explain: Scheduled prompts turn a repeated request into an automation - for example a weekly summary of a project - running on a schedule and delivering the results back in Copilot. They require a Copilot licence and connected experiences to be enabled.

wrong.0: Capacity is handled by billing policies, not prompts.
wrong.2: There is no prompt approval workflow of this kind.
wrong.3: Copilot can help schedule a meeting, but that is not what scheduled prompts are.

questions.q: Your company has bought contoso.com and wants to use it for email and sign-in. Where do you add the domain and prove you own it?
questions.explain: Domains are tenant-level, so they sit under Settings. Adding one here gives you the DNS records to publish, and the tenant will not use the domain until that verification passes.

questions.q: Leadership wants the company address updated and the tenant switched to targeted release so they see new features early. Where do you go?
questions.explain: Org settings holds the organisation profile — name, address, contact details — and the release preferences that decide how early the tenant receives new features.

questions.q: Forty people should receive a copy of anything sent to allstaff@contoso.com in their own mailbox. Where do you create that object?
questions.explain: A distribution group fans a message out to every member's personal mailbox, and distribution groups live under Recipients alongside the other things that can receive mail.

questions.q: A supplier says an invoice email never arrived. You need to follow that one specific message through the service. Where do you look?
questions.explain: Message trace follows an individual message end to end and shows where it was delivered, deferred, filtered or dropped. It answers 'what happened to this one email?'

questions.q: External people must no longer be addable to any team. Where do you turn that off?
questions.explain: Guest access controls whether people from outside the tenant can be added into teams at all, and what they can do once inside. It is the switch that stops guests being added anywhere.

questions.q: The executive team should be allowed to record meetings while everyone else is not. Where do you configure that?
questions.explain: Policies are how Teams applies different settings to different people. You build a meeting policy with the settings you want and assign it to those users or a group, leaving everyone else on the global default.

questions.q: Six users cannot sign in this morning and you need the exact failure code and which policy was applied for each attempt. Where do you look?
questions.explain: Sign-in logs record every authentication attempt: the status, the failure code, the device and location, and the conditional access policies that evaluated. That is what separates an MFA problem from a policy block.

questions.q: Finance staff must be prompted for MFA whenever they reach the payroll app from outside the office. Where is this rule built?
questions.explain: Conditional Access is the if-then policy engine: it reads signals such as user, app, device, location and risk, then grants, blocks, or grants with a requirement like MFA attached.

questions.q: You want your admins to hold no standing privilege — they should activate a role only when they need it, with approval and an expiry. Where do you set that up?
questions.explain: Privileged Identity Management turns standing role assignments into eligible ones. Admins activate when needed, optionally with justification, approval and MFA, and access expires on its own.

questions.q: Your manager asks how the tenant's identity configuration compares with Microsoft's recommended practice, as a percentage. Where do you find it?
questions.explain: Identity Secure Score scores your identity configuration against Microsoft's recommendations and lists prioritised improvement actions with the points each one is worth.

questions.q: A third-party app is already in use in the tenant and you need to review the consent it holds and control who may sign in to it. Where do you go?
questions.explain: The enterprise application is that app's presence in your tenant — its service principal. It is where consent, user and group assignment, and single sign-on are managed. App registrations, by contrast, define an application you own.

questions.q: Before switching Copilot on, you need to find which sites are shared with 'Everyone except external users'. Where do you look?
questions.explain: Data access governance reports surface exactly this exposure: sites shared broadly with the whole organisation, sharing-link hotspots and permission baselines. It is the standard first step of Copilot readiness.

questions.q: A board site must be openable only by members of one Entra security group, even by people who were granted access to it previously. Where do you enforce that?
questions.explain: Restricted access control draws a hard boundary around the site: only members of the nominated group get in, regardless of earlier permissions or sharing links.

questions.q: A legal team's site must keep working normally for them, but must never appear in Copilot answers or organisation-wide search. Where do you configure that?
questions.explain: Restricted content discovery removes a site from Copilot and tenant-wide search while leaving its permissions untouched — the team carries on working, the content simply stops surfacing elsewhere.

questions.q: You have a list of overshared sites and want each site's own owner to confirm or remove the access rather than doing it centrally. Where do you start that?
questions.explain: Site access reviews push the decision to the people who understand the content. You flag sites from a governance report and their owners review and clean up the access.

questions.q: A policy has fired several times overnight and you need to see which sensitive data was involved, which user, and what action was taken. Where do you go?
questions.explain: The DLP alerts queue shows each match with the policy that fired, the sensitive information found, the user, and whether the action was blocked, overridden or just audited — and lets you set an investigation status.

questions.q: You want a report showing which SharePoint sites hold sensitive data and are broadly shared, specifically to size up the risk before a Copilot rollout. Where do you go?
questions.explain: Data risk assessments in DSPM for AI scan for potentially overshared items containing sensitive information. A default assessment runs weekly over your busiest sites, and you can build custom ones.

questions.q: You want to stop users pasting customer national ID numbers into AI prompts, using a ready-made policy rather than building one from scratch. Where do you go?
questions.explain: DSPM for AI ships one-click policies, including DLP applied to AI prompts. That is what blocks sensitive information from being submitted to Copilot and other AI apps.

questions.q: Legal needs every email, document and Teams message mentioning 'Project Harrier' across the whole tenant, ready to export. Where do you run that?
questions.explain: Content search queries mailboxes, sites, OneDrive and Teams with keywords and conditions, then lets you preview and export what it finds for the case.

questions.q: You need to know which administrator changed an external sharing setting three weeks ago. Where do you look?
questions.explain: The unified audit log records user and admin activity across the Microsoft 365 workloads. Search it by date range, activity type and user to find who did what and when.

questions.q: You want a current snapshot of every item in the tenant carrying a sensitivity label or a detected sensitive information type, and where those items are stored. Where do you go?
questions.explain: Data explorer gives you the inventory: what is labelled or classified right now, and in which sites, mailboxes and accounts it sits. It answers 'what sensitive data do we have and where?'

questions.q: Someone downgraded a Confidential label on a contract last week and you need the history of label actions to find out who. Where do you look?
questions.explain: Activity explorer is the historical view of what people did with labelled content — labels applied, changed or removed, files copied, DLP rules matched — over time.

questions.q: Finance records must be kept for seven years across all SharePoint sites and then deleted automatically. Where do you configure this?
questions.explain: A retention policy applies to whole locations, so pointing one at SharePoint covers every site inside it. Retention labels, by contrast, are applied to individual items.

questions.q: A policy has flagged messages for potentially harassing language and a reviewer must now read them in context and decide. Where do they go?
questions.explain: Flagged messages land in the Communication Compliance review queue, where a designated reviewer sees the message in context and resolves, tags, notifies or escalates it.

questions.q: HR has written a set of standard prompts they want suggested to everyone inside Copilot Chat and Teams. Where do you publish them?
questions.explain: Organisational prompts are created and published under Copilot > Prompts, then surface to users as suggested prompts, in the prompt lab, and as typeahead suggestions. AI Administrator or Search Editor can do this.

questions.q: Only the Finance department should be able to use agents; everybody else should have no access. Where do you scope that?
questions.explain: Agent access sits in the Copilot settings, under data access. You choose all users, no users, or specific users and groups, and you can also restrict which publishers of agents are permitted.

questions.q: A maker has published an agent from Copilot Studio to the organisation and it is waiting on you. Where do you review and approve it?
questions.explain: Publishing to the organisation creates a request rather than a live agent. You review its data and tools, its security and compliance details, and then publish it to the catalogue or reject it.

questions.q: You want a list of every agent in the tenant so you can filter for the ones that have no owner and clean them up. Where do you go?
questions.explain: The agent inventory lists every agent with its publisher, availability and supported products, and includes a 'missing an owner' filter for finding abandoned agents.

questions.q: Pay-as-you-go agent spend is climbing and you need to set a budget alert and a hard cap. Where do you go?
questions.explain: Cost management is where pay-as-you-go consumption is tracked and controlled: billing policies, budgets with email alerts at spending thresholds, and hard caps that stop consumption rather than letting it overrun.

questions.q: Fifty new starters all need a Microsoft 365 Copilot licence in one go. Where do you assign them in bulk?
questions.explain: The Licenses page handles assignment across many users at once. You can also assign one at a time under Active users, or attach the licence to a group and let group-based licensing do it.

questions.q: You need to know how many of the assigned Copilot licences are actually being used each month, broken down by app. Where do you look?
questions.explain: The Copilot usage report shows enabled users, active users and activity per app — Teams, Word, Outlook, Excel, PowerPoint — which is how you spot idle licences worth reassigning.

questions.q: Agents built in Copilot Studio need governance applied to the environments that hold them. Where do you go?
questions.explain: Copilot Studio agents live inside Power Platform environments, so environment governance, capacity and settings are managed from the Power Platform admin center.

questions.q: You must stop makers building an agent that combines a business connector with a social media connector. Where do you set that restriction?
questions.explain: Data policies define which connectors may be used together, so a maker cannot wire company data through to an unapproved destination in an agent or a flow.

questions.q: You need to decide whether users are allowed to upload their own custom apps and agents into Teams. Where is that switch?
questions.explain: Setup policies control pinned apps and the sideloading permission — whether a user may upload a custom app or agent package into Teams themselves.
